# 2 Maccabees Chapter 5 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 5 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_005_page_001.jpg

---

## Preamble

Chapter 5 marks the catastrophic turn. Antiochus IV's second Egyptian campaign (168 BCE) is interrupted by the false rumor of his death, triggering Jason's failed coup. Antiochus then sacks Jerusalem with extraordinary violence, desecrates the temple, and installs oppressive governors. The chapter closes with Judas Maccabeus's withdrawal into the wilderness — a note of hope that will sustain the remainder of the book. The three agents agree on narrative structure but diverge on the celestial vision (vv. 2–3), the theological commentary (vv. 17–20), and the register of the massacre (vv. 13–14).

---

**1** About this time Antiochus undertook his second campaign against Egypt.

**2** And it happened that throughout the city, for nearly forty days, there appeared in the air riders on horseback in golden armor, and armed formations in full battle array of spears and swords —

**3** companies of cavalry drawn up, charges and countercharges on both sides, the brandishing of shields, formations of spears, the flight of arrows, flashing golden ornaments, and armor of every kind.

**4** So all men prayed that this apparition would prove to be a good omen.

**5** But a false rumor arose that Antiochus had died. Jason took no fewer than a thousand men and made a surprise attack upon the city. When the forces on the wall had been pushed back and the city was being overrun, Menelaus took refuge in the citadel.

**6** But Jason kept massacring his own fellow citizens without mercy, not perceiving that success against one's own kinsmen is the worst of failures, but thinking that he was setting up trophies over enemies and not over fellow countrymen.

**7** Nevertheless he did not gain control of the government. In the end he received only disgrace from his conspiracy, and went again as a fugitive into the country of the Ammonites.

**8** Finally he came to a miserable end. Accused before Aretas the ruler of the Arabs, fleeing from city to city, hunted by everyone, hated as a rebel against the laws and abhorred as the butcher of his country and his fellow citizens, he was cast ashore in Egypt;

**9** and he who had driven many from their homeland into exile died in exile himself, having embarked to go to the Lacedaemonians in hope of finding protection there on account of their supposed kinship.

**10** He who had cast out many to lie unburied had no one to mourn for him. He had no funeral of any kind and no burial place in the tombs of his ancestors.

**11** When news of what had occurred reached the king, he concluded that Judea was in revolt. Raging in spirit, he departed from Egypt and took the city by force.

**12** He commanded his soldiers to cut down without mercy those whom they encountered and to slaughter those who had taken refuge in their houses.

**13** There was a massacre of young and old alike, a destruction of women and children, a slaughter of virgins and infants.

**14** Within three days, eighty thousand perished — forty thousand in hand-to-hand fighting, and as many more sold into slavery.

**15** Not content with this, he had the audacity to enter the most holy temple in all the world, with Menelaus — who had turned traitor both to the laws and to his country — as his guide.

**16** With his defiled hands he seized the sacred vessels, and with his profane hands swept away what other kings had dedicated for the exaltation, glory, and honor of the place.

**17** Antiochus was puffed up with pride, not perceiving that the LORD had been provoked to anger for a brief time because of the sins of those who dwelt in the city, and that this was why the place had been left unguarded.

**18** But had they not been already enmeshed in many sins, this man would have been scourged and turned back from his presumption the moment he came forward — just as Heliodorus was, when King Seleucus sent him to inspect the treasury.

**19** But God did not choose the nation for the sake of the holy place; he chose the place for the sake of the nation.

**20** Therefore the holy place itself shared in the misfortunes that befell the nation and afterward participated in its good fortune; and what was forsaken in the wrath of the Almighty was restored again in all its glory when the great LORD was reconciled.

**21** So Antiochus, having carried off eighteen hundred talents from the temple, hurried back to Antioch, thinking in his arrogance that he could make the land navigable and the sea passable on foot — so exalted was his mind.

**22** He left governors to oppress the nation: at Jerusalem, Philip, a Phrygian by birth and in character more barbarous than the man who appointed him;

**23** at Gerizim, Andronicus; and besides these Menelaus, who treated the citizens more harshly than the others. In his hatred of the Jewish people,

**24** Antiochus dispatched Apollonius, the commander of the Mysians, with an army of twenty-two thousand, with orders to kill all the grown men and to sell the women and young.

**25** When Apollonius arrived in Jerusalem, he made a pretense of peaceful intentions and waited until the holy sabbath day. Then, finding the Jews at rest, he ordered his men to parade under arms.

**26** All those who came out to watch he struck down with the sword. Then he rushed into the city with his armed men and killed great numbers.

**27** But Judas Maccabeus, with about nine others, withdrew into the wilderness and lived in the mountains like wild animals with his companions, feeding on what grew there, so that they might have no share in the defilement.

---

## Translator's Notes

- **vv. 2–3, the celestial vision**: Heavenly cavalry before a great battle is a common omen in Hellenistic and Jewish literature (cf. 2 Macc 10:29, 11:8). The vision is deliberately ambiguous — the people pray it is a good omen, but it is not.
- **v. 6, "setting up trophies"**: The *tropaion* (trophy) in Greek warfare was a monument erected on the spot where the enemy turned to flee. Jason's "trophies" over his own countrymen is a bitter irony.
- **v. 9, Lacedaemonians/Spartans**: A tradition claimed kinship between Sparta and the Jews (cf. 1 Macc 12:21). Jason's appeal to this kinship for asylum marks his complete isolation and desperation.
- **vv. 17–20, theological commentary**: This is one of the most significant theological passages in 2 Maccabees. The author insists that Antiochus's success was not a sign of God's absence but of God's disciplinary anger — and, crucially, that God chose the place for the nation, not the nation for the place. This reverses a common assumption about the temple's primacy.
- **v. 27, Judas in the wilderness**: The wilderness withdrawal echoes prophetic typology (Moses, Elijah). Judas emerges as a figure of pure resistance who will not compromise with the defilement even for survival.
